content:
President Donald Trump said on Saturday that he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates at 10 percent, reviving a promise from his 2024 campaign that stalled under Republican control of Congress and setting up one of the most unlikely political alliances of his second term.

"I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot," Trump told Fox News Channel's "Saturday in America," according to [the Associated Press](https://beta.manilatimes.net/2026/11/22/world/trump-vows-to-work-with-democrats-to-cap-credit-card-interest-rates-at-10/2475574/amp). The standard proposal, backed by Democrats and the president alike, would cut the ceiling on what card issuers can charge to 10 percent — less than half the rate most borrowers pay today.

The scale of the change is what makes the pledge so politically potent. The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2 percent, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve, and Federal Reserve data released in November put the average rate on accounts assessed interest at 22.36 percent in the third quarter of 2026, with many cards — especially those issued to consumers with lower credit scores — charging well above 25 percent. Researchers who studied Trump's campaign pledge after it was first announced found that Americans would save roughly $100 billion a year in interest if rates were capped at 10 percent.

For an individual household, the arithmetic is stark. A family carrying a $5,000 balance at 22 percent accrues about $1,100 in interest over a year; at 10 percent, the same balance costs about $500. The roughly $600 difference is the kind of money that decides whether a household pays down its balance or watches it grow — and it is why the proposal, first floated in September 2024 on the campaign trail, has survived two years of industry opposition.

What has changed is the politics. In the November 3 midterm elections, Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate, and the new majorities will take over when the next Congress convenes in January 2027. Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, who is expected to become chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has said repeatedly that she wants to cap rates, and she responded to Trump's interview within hours. "Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money," Warren said. Representative Maxine Waters of California, a senior Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee, has also endorsed the idea.

The alliance is unusual enough to be the story in itself. Warren is one of Trump's fiercest critics, and the credit card cap would pair her with a president whose party spent the last two years showing little interest in the idea. Trump acknowledged as much on Saturday, saying he had been unable to deliver on the promise because of industry pressure and a lack of interest from his fellow Republicans. The bill that would actually create the cap has existed for nearly two years without moving: in February 2025, Senators Bernie Sanders and Josh Hawley introduced the 10 Percent Credit Card Interest Rate Cap Act, which would hold rates at 10 percent for five years, while Representatives Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Anna Paulina Luna introduced a companion bill in the House. Neither has passed.

There are also hard limits on what Trump can do on his own. As [a legal analysis by Nolo](https://www.nolo.com/legal-encyclopedia/can-president-trump-legally-cap-credit-card-interest-rates-at-10.html) notes, the president has no authority to impose a nationwide cap without new legislation from Congress — or an agreement from the card companies themselves. Trump has already tested that boundary once: in January, he posted on Truth Social calling for a one-year cap at 10 percent and later said at the World Economic Forum in Davos that he was "asking Congress to cap credit card interest rates at 10% for one year." Nothing binding followed, and no bill has been introduced in the new Congress.

That leaves two open questions that will decide whether the pledge becomes law. The first is timing: Democrats do not take control until January, so no vote can happen before then, and the new Congress will have a crowded agenda. The second is duration: Trump's January proposal was for a one-year cap, while the Sanders-Hawley bill would run for five years, and neither Trump nor congressional Democrats have said which version they would pursue.

The industry's resistance, which helped kill the idea under Republican control, has not gone away. Card issuers argue that a 10 percent ceiling would force them to tighten lending, particularly to borrowers with weaker credit, and to scale back rewards programmes that are funded by interest income. Consumer advocates answer that rates near 22 percent already function as a tax on households that can least afford it, and that the $100 billion in annual savings estimated by researchers would flow overwhelmingly to lower- and middle-income borrowers.

Whether the unlikely coalition holds past the first weeks of the new Congress is the real test. Trump has now publicly committed to working with Democrats on a policy his own party resisted, Warren has publicly accepted the invitation, and a bipartisan bill already exists to carry it. For the tens of millions of Americans paying interest at more than twice the proposed cap, the question is no longer whether the idea has supporters in Washington — it is whether supporters on opposite sides of the aisle can agree on a bill before the politics of the moment passes. Trump, who has made affordability the centrepiece of his domestic agenda this year — including [signing the Epstein Files Transparency Act into law this week](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/trump-signs-epstein-files-transparency-act-november-2026) after a bruising fight with Congress — will be judged on whether this promise, unlike the January version, ends in legislation rather than a post. The president's diplomacy has dominated the headlines this month, from [the trilateral summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/xi-trump-putin-summit-shenzhen-november-19), but the credit card cap may prove the more consequential test of his ability to govern with a Congress his party no longer controls.
summary: President Donald Trump said on Saturday he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates at 10 percent, down from a median of about 22 percent; Senator Elizabeth Warren, expected to chair the Senate Banking Committee, swiftly backed the plan, but no bill can pass before the new Congress convenes in January 2027.
title: Trump vows to work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates at 10%
